openers.working-lands: Food systems cause one third of human greenhouse gas emissions, so how land is farmed shapes the planet. This chapter turns from wild places to working ones: fields, pastures and orchards. Farming leaves by-products that pollute water, air and soil, and it can strip topsoil and fertility. A family of approaches tries to do better, from changing crops season by season and leaving soil unplowed to growing plants just to cover the ground. Some aim only to sustain the land, while others aim to rebuild its soil, biodiversity and ecosystem services.

nature-nbs-235.title: Sustainable agriculture: farming that can last
nature-nbs-235.text: Food systems cause one third of human greenhouse gas emissions. Agriculture's footprint is huge, and sustainable agriculture tries to shrink it. It is farming that reduces harm to the environment, maintains and builds up natural resources, and uses non-renewable resources productively. The aim is to produce crops or livestock without damaging soil, water, biodiversity, or the people on and near the farm. Its toolkit can include {{ref:nature-nbs-297}}, growing trees among crops, mixed farming, multiple cropping and rotating crops from season to season. In 1977 the USDA defined it as practices that, over the long term, meet food needs, improve the environment, use resources efficiently, keep farms viable and improve farmers' quality of life. Economics explains part of the problem. Environmental costs left out of a farmer's ordinary accounts are externalities, so the market does not punish them. Investment in sustainable farming is said to be four times more cost-effective than direct food aid. Yet it gets only three percent of humanitarian funds. Many certification systems exist, including organic labels, Rainforest Alliance and Fair Trade. People still disagree on what sustainability means here. An ecocentric view favors low growth and organic methods. A technocentric view relies on technology and modified industry.

nature-nbs-310.title: Soil health: judging soil as a living system
nature-nbs-310.text: Some microbiologists believe 80% of soil nutrient functions are controlled by microbes. That belief explains a shift in how people judge the ground. Soil health is the state of a soil that performs the full range of ecosystem functions suited to its environment. It arises from good interactions among a soil's living and non-living parts, such as microbes, plants and animals. It covers sustaining productivity, biodiversity, water and air quality, and human health. The term has largely replaced soil quality, which judged soil for one purpose only, such as growing maize. Soil health depends on soil biodiversity. It improves when soil is kept covered and given carbon-rich amendments. The stakes are real. US soils have lost up to 75% of their carbon over 40 years, though how much is debated. Definitions are contested too. A soil can be healthy for ecosystems without directly serving crops, so scientists still debate how to define and measure it.

nature-nbs-226.title: Carbon farming: pulling carbon from the air into soil
nature-nbs-226.text: Turning a forest, grassland or savanna into cropland cuts the soil's organic carbon by about 30–40%. Carbon farming tries to run that process in reverse. It is a set of farming and forestry methods meant to store carbon from the air in soil and living plants. The overall goal is a net removal of carbon from the atmosphere, by speeding up how fast carbon is locked away. Methods include changing tillage and grazing, using mulch or compost, adding biochar and changing which crops are grown. Biochar, a charcoal mixed into soil, locks away roughly 50% of the carbon in the original biomass. The potential is large. Carbon farming could offset as much as 20% of 2010 carbon dioxide emissions each year, and by 2016 its variants covered hundreds of millions of hectares. Farmers who store carbon can sell credits to companies that need offsets, as in Australia. But the storage is not permanent. Disturbing the soil or tilling hard turns it back into a source of greenhouse gases. If incentives reward only stored carbon, they could encourage land clearing, single-crop farming and biodiversity loss. The effect on crop yields is unsettled, and critics doubt the practices can spread widely enough to matter.

nature-nbs-276.title: Crop rotation: changing what grows, season by season
nature-nbs-276.text: Plant the same crop year after year and the soil tires of it. Growing one crop repeatedly, called monocropping, drains particular nutrients and breeds specialized pests. Crop rotation is the fix: growing a sequence of different crops on the same land over successive seasons. It stops crops drawing on one set of nutrients and reduces pests, weeds and resistance. Changing crops interrupts pest life cycles and habitat. Rotating nitrogen-fixing legumes such as clover with nitrogen-hungry crops supplies nitrogen to the crops that follow. Rotations, especially diverse long ones, greatly increase soil organic carbon. Different crops also spread the farmer's risk from bad weather. During the Green Revolution, developed countries largely replaced rotation with chemical fertilizers. Today US organic certification requires it.

nature-nbs-267.title: Agricultural pollution: farming's spillover
nature-nbs-267.text: Runoff from farms, gathered in large water bodies, creates dead zones downstream. Agricultural pollution is contamination or damage to the environment, people or their livelihoods from the by-products of farming. Some comes from single discharge points. More often it comes from diffuse non-point sources spread across the landscape, and from air pollution. The list of pollutants is long: sediments, nutrients, pathogens, pesticides, metals and salts. They reach lakes, rivers, wetlands, estuaries and groundwater. Poor management drives much of it, such as overgrazing, plowing and badly timed pesticide use. Animal agriculture has an outsized impact on the pollutants entering the environment. Economists see the problem as an externality, a cost the farmer does not pay. So agricultural economists design incentives to control it, for example to curb water pollution from farms.

nature-nbs-305.title: Soil conservation: keeping topsoil and fertility
nature-nbs-305.text: Each one percent increase in soil organic matter lets soil hold 20,000 gallons more water per acre. Soil conservation protects that capacity. It means preventing the loss of topsoil to erosion and the loss of fertility from overuse, acidification, salinization or contamination. Deforestation typically causes large-scale erosion, nutrient loss and sometimes desertification. Farmers have practiced conservation for millennia. Techniques include rotating crops, growing plants to cover bare soil, tilling less and planting tree rows against the wind. The EU's Common Agricultural Policy promotes reduced tillage, winter cover, plant residues and grass margins. Farming methods alone are not enough. Solving erosion also needs political and economic action, including changing how land is valued. Taxing pesticides at different rates is one option studied.

nature-nbs-258.title: Regenerative agriculture: farming to rebuild, not just sustain
nature-nbs-258.text: An estimated 30–75% of global soil organic matter has been lost since tillage-based farming began. Regenerative agriculture aims to win some of it back. It seeks to restore rather than just sustain, rebuilding topsoil, biodiversity and ecosystem services. It is not one practice but a mix of sustainable techniques, such as recycling farm waste and adding compost. The Rodale Institute began using the term in the early 1980s. A 2020 review of 229 articles and 25 websites found no legal or broadly accepted definition. Its four most consistent principles are improving soil health, optimizing resource use, easing climate change and improving water. A 2023 review found practices like reduced tillage and growing trees on farms can help soil carbon or yields in some conditions, but evidence is limited. Some scientists call the climate claims, especially for grazing, exaggerated.

nature-nbs-290.title: No-till farming: growing crops without plowing
nature-nbs-290.text: In Argentina, skipping the plow cut erosion losses by 80% and costs by more than 50%. No-till farming grows crops or pasture without disturbing the soil by tillage. It is also called zero tillage or direct drilling. It reduces erosion, especially on sandy, dry, sloping soils, and can improve water infiltration, organic matter and nutrient cycling. Fewer machinery passes lower fuel and labor costs, and in Paraguay net farm incomes rose 77%. Worldwide area grew from about 45 million ha in 1999 to 111 million ha in 2009. There are trade-offs. Without tillage to remove weeds, farmers commonly use herbicides such as glyphosate. Cold, wet spring soil can delay planting. Whether no-till really raises soil carbon is debated, since some studies suspect flawed testing. England's DEFRA pays farmers £73 per hectare to convert.

nature-nbs-297.title: Permaculture: designing farms like ecosystems
nature-nbs-297.text: In 1978 Bill Mollison and David Holmgren coined a word as a challenge to industrial farming. Permaculture is an approach to designing land use and settlements that copies the arrangements found in thriving natural ecosystems. It rests on design principles from whole-systems thinking, applied to farming, town planning, rewilding and community resilience. Earlier ideas of permanent agriculture inspired it, such as F. H. King's 1911 book and J. Russell Smith's Tree Crops of 1929. Holmgren set out twelve principles, among them observe and interact, catch and store energy, and obtain a yield. It favors perennial crops that need no yearly tilling and planting. Critics say it is loosely defined and largely isolated from scientific literature.

nature-nbs-255.title: Cover crops: plants grown to protect the soil
nature-nbs-255.text: Some crops are never meant for the market. A cover crop is a plant grown to cover the soil rather than to be harvested. Often its only job is to stop erosion: roots anchor soil and the canopy slows raindrops and runoff. Cover crops also help manage fertility, water, weeds, pests, diseases and wildlife. A meta-analysis of 102 field studies found they raised topsoil organic carbon by about 10% and nitrogen by about 20%. They reduce water pollution and take carbon dioxide out of the air. Thick stands smother weeds, and some suppress them chemically through allelopathy. In one study, songbird densities were 7–20 times higher in cotton fields with a clover cover. But effects on the next crop's water and yield vary, and long-term profitability is uncertain.

nature-nbs-286.title: Intercropping: two crops, one field, same time
nature-nbs-286.text: A single crop leaves some light, water and nutrients unused. Intercropping is growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture. Its main goal is a larger total yield from those leftover resources. Crops are paired so they do not compete: deep roots with shallow, tall plants with shade-tolerant ones. A companion crop can prop up plants prone to falling over, or supply nutrients. In low-input systems it can give higher yields for the same input. Results vary, though. A 2008 review found pest predators rose in only 53% of studies and yields in only 32%. Crop rotation differs because its crops grow in separate seasons.

nature-nbs-246.title: Agroecology: ecology applied to the farm
nature-nbs-246.text: Organic farming is practiced in 188 countries, and it is one of three certified forms of agroecology. Agroecology is the study and practice of applying ecological processes to farming, looking at links between plants, animals, people and the environment. The term can mean a science, a set of practices, or a social movement. It draws on agronomy, ecology, sociology, economics and history. It studies farm ecosystems' productivity, stability, sustainability and fairness, at scales from a gene to the globe. Unlike in natural ecology, human activity and economics are the main forces at work. Biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food are its certified varieties. Movements such as La Via Campesina use it to pursue food sovereignty. Researchers heatedly debate which model of farming policy should support.

nature-nbs-247.title: Agroforestry: trees and crops on the same ground
nature-nbs-247.text: Of over 700 East African households surveyed, at least 50% had begun planting trees to adapt to climate change. They were practicing agroforestry, a way of managing land that grows trees together with crops or pasture on the same ground. Forester John Bene coined the term in 1973, but the practice is millennia old. It uses the forest as a model, managing land to make the most of helpful interactions between plants and animals. That is why it is described as applied agroecology. The harvest can be broad: timber, fruit, nuts, mushrooms, medicinal plants and animals. Growing varied products such as fuelwood and medicinal plants makes farm income more secure. Well managed, it raises productivity and profits, reduces soil erosion, provides wildlife habitat and boosts biodiversity. Trees store carbon in soil and wood and can recapture some carbon lost when forests were cut. Agroforestry is most common on tropical smallholdings, especially in sub-Saharan Africa, and has spread to the US and Europe.

nature-nbs-233.title: Landscape-scale conservation: managing the whole picture
nature-nbs-233.text: A river basin supplies water, timber, crops and habitat, and each use affects the others. Landscape-scale conservation manages the whole landscape to balance nature against farming, forestry and other uses of the same land. It is an alternative to protecting single sites. Its backers argue that poverty, food security, climate change, water scarcity and biodiversity loss are linked and need coordinated action. Rather than serve one land use, it tries to meet many stakeholders' interests. The IUCN applied it in 27 landscapes in 23 countries. In 2015 UNEP described this landscape approach as embodying ecosystem management. A review found five barriers, including confusing terms, long delays before action and sectors working in silos.

nature-nbs-260.title: Riparian buffers: green strips that guard streams
nature-nbs-260.text: A nine-year University of Georgia study found streamside buffers removed at least 60% of nitrogen and 65% of phosphorus from fertilizer runoff. A riparian buffer is a strip of vegetation, usually trees, along a stream that shades it and shields it from nearby land use. Buffers catch sediment, nutrients and pesticides before they reach the water. They counter eutrophication downstream and stabilize banks. They also provide habitat and wildlife corridors in farm country. Buffers can raise land value and grow profitable crops such as black walnut and hazelnut. Programs such as the US Conservation Reserve Program pay farmers for the land taken out of production. They have limits: a 2017 study found little ability to stop glyphosate leaching to streams.

nature-nbs-238.title: Land sharing: making room for wildlife on the farm
nature-nbs-238.text: One answer to farming's pressure on nature is to blend the two. Land sharing, also called wildlife-friendly agriculture, makes room for biodiversity inside farmed areas by farming less intensively. Growing trees among crops and mixing crops with livestock are examples. Reviews more often find it better for food security and livelihoods, in 58% of studies. That strength sets up its rivalry with the opposite strategy.

nature-nbs-237.title: Land sparing: farm hard here so nature can stay wild there
nature-nbs-237.text: For over 150 years, developed countries have mostly kept farms and nature apart. That strategy is land sparing. It farms some land intensively for high yields so that other land can stay wild. Strict separation is the point. Reviews find it generally favored for conserving tropical forest biodiversity, in 67% of relevant studies. Its strength lies in protecting wild habitat, while sharing does better for farm livelihoods.

nature-nbs-239.title: Sparing or sharing: how should farms and nature divide land?
nature-nbs-239.text: Should nature be fenced off from farms or woven into them? Scientists have argued over this for more than a decade without a clear consensus. Land sparing keeps the two strictly apart, farming some land intensively so other land stays wild. Land sharing mixes them, farming less intensively so wildlife can live among the crops. Each wins on different measures. Sparing tends to win for tropical forest biodiversity. Sharing tends to win for food security and livelihoods. That split suggests no single answer fits everywhere. Because each strategy's success depends on the landscape, a third option has been proposed: {{ref:nature-nbs-240}}, a mix of the two. The debate remains open.

nature-nbs-236.title: Sustainable intensification: more food without more land
nature-nbs-236.text: By 2018 an estimated 163 million farms in 100 nations used sustainable intensification, on 453 million ha, or 29% of farms worldwide. It means farming methods that raise production while also improving environmental outcomes, without clearing more land. That weight on environmental results sets it apart from earlier intensification. A striking example comes from east Asian rice fields. Nectar plants that support pest predators cut insecticide need by 70% with a 5% yield gain. Still, whether ecosystem services can replace non-renewable inputs while keeping yields high has been much debated.

nature-nbs-280.title: Hedges: living boundaries that shelter wildlife
nature-nbs-280.text: The first hedges enclosed cereal fields in the Neolithic, 4000–6000 years ago. A hedge is a line of shrubs, sometimes with trees, planted and trained as a barrier or boundary; old field-boundary hedges are called hedgerows. They often shelter crops from wind. They also help prevent soil loss, reduce pollution, regulate water and reduce flooding. One study found 100% of northwest European farms have hedges, providing 43% of the wildlife habitat there. Removing them makes bigger, cheaper-to-farm fields with more yield and profit, but weakens soil and causes erosion. After World War II, UK hedge removal was subsidized, and over half of UK hedgerows have vanished since the 1950s. Now the government increasingly pays farmers to maintain them.
